ui.metaDescription: Playhead: interpretable overview strips and analysis-driven effects for music and game audio, running entirely in the browser.
ui.title: Playhead waveform lab
ui.intro: A waveform shows a sound's level. Playhead adds what the sound is doing (its intensity, character, rhythm and structure) as curves, marks and a spectrogram on the waveform's own time axis. Compare the views, compose a strip of your own, and try the effects bench, whose tools act on the events and curves the analysis finds rather than on fixed frequencies. Thirteen game sound effects and three music test signals with known structure are built in; drop your own WAV, OGG, MP3 or FLAC files to compare. Nothing leaves this tab.
ui.translationComment.title: Suggest a better word or report a mistake; opens a form on GitHub
ui.englishTerms.title: In explanations, show the English term in brackets after technical terms
ui.thumb.auto: By class: D5 for SFX, D4 otherwise
sec.today.title: Today
sec.today.desc: What the Unity inspector draws now: min and max per channel, linear, left on top.
sec.single.title: Single curves
sec.single.desc: Each strip is one curve: a candidate for the line an editor could draw instead of the waveform.
sec.single.readme: Reading the badge. The number is how closely the curve's ups and downs follow loudness's, from 0 (unrelated) to 1 (moving in lockstep). Technically: the correlation between the two curves' column-to-column changes, over 400 columns with silence left out. moves on its own under 0.3, partly follows loudness 0.3 to 0.6, follows loudness 0.6 and above. A low number only says the curve is different, not that it is useful: random noise would also score near 0. The times next to it are where the curve sits furthest above loudness; click one and listen to judge whether that difference is real.
sec.sfx.title: Short sound effects
sec.sfx.desc: What a 0.5 to 5 s sound is made of. Clips under 6 s are analysed every 2.9 ms instead of 11.6 ms, so a 5 ms click keeps its shape.
sec.rhythm.title: Rhythm and events
sec.rhythm.desc: Where things happen. On the built-in signals the beat rows are scored against the true beats: F-measure with ±70 ms tolerance, where 1.00 means every beat found and nothing extra.
sec.structure.title: Structure
sec.structure.desc: Sections found by comparing every moment with every other moment. A letter repeats when material returns.
sec.desc.title: Cross-field descriptors
sec.desc.desc: Measures borrowed from machine diagnostics, seismology, ecoacoustics, voice science, optimal transport, information theory and impact acoustics. Most have a fixed value for noise or a steady tone, so the built-in descriptor tour shows each one doing exactly what the maths says.
sec.design.title: Combined strips
sec.design.desc: Height carries the main curve and colour a second one, on a ramp that gets lighter as the value rises. These are the candidates for the actual preview.
sec.compose.title: Compose your own
sec.compose.desc: Choose what goes on one strip: the waveform or a spectrogram behind, a colour, a line, up to three curves as separate waveform-like shapes or overlaid on the waveform, and the marks. The ordinary waveform and spectrogram are drawn underneath for comparison. The result is a look code that SFX Workbench and kurator understand, so a combination found here can be used there, and sent with your feedback.
sec.bench.title: Effects bench
sec.bench.desc: Processing driven by the analysis. Each result joins the library and is analysed like any other file, so every view above can compare it with the original.
sec.library.title: Library
sec.library.desc: Every loaded file at thumbnail size on one absolute scale. Click a row to inspect it above.
sec.matrix.title: How the curves relate
sec.matrix.desc: Correlation of column-to-column changes for the selected file, 400 columns, silent columns left out. Values near 1 mean two curves move together and one of them is redundant on this material.
sec.guide.title: Curve guide
sec.guide.desc: What each curve should reveal and where it is expected to mislead. Formulas and sources are in the research report.
note.builtin.title: Built-in signals
note.builtin.text: The SFX kit is 13 synthetic game sounds from 0.5 to 4 s, from a UI click to an explosion with debris, plus one file exported with typical faults. Each has known events and tags, and X5 scores against them. The probe suite holds loudness at −20 LUFS while character changes, so C1 stays flat and every other curve has to earn its movement. The cue arc is a 64 s, 120 BPM track with an intro, groove, build, drop, breakdown and outro; its beats, downbeats and sections are known. The tempo ramp accelerates from 96 to 144 BPM over 32 s, which a single-tempo beat tracker cannot follow.
note.approx.title: Approximations in this prototype
note.approx.1: Sone values use the ISO 532-1 core formula on 24 Bark bands with a Terhardt threshold, not the full standard. Sharpness uses DIN 45692 weighting.
note.approx.2: Roughness is the 30–150 Hz envelope modulation share in 12 bands, calibrated so a 1 kHz, 60 dB tone with 100% AM at 70 Hz reads 1 asper. Fluctuation is calibrated the same way at 4 Hz.
note.approx.3: Composite weights, the 25 s tension leak and the library reference ranges are starting values tuned on the built-in signals, not published constants.
note.approx.4: Curves are not delayed to match listener response lag; that lag belongs to the ratings, not the sound.
note.rhythm.title: Rhythm and structure methods
note.rhythm.1: The rhythm onset envelope compresses mel energies with log(1 + 300·E/E<sub>local</sub>), so quiet hats count less than loud kicks, and gives low, mid and high frequencies equal weight.
note.rhythm.2: Tempo comes from an 8 s autocorrelation tempogram with a one-octave prior around 120 BPM, as in librosa. R2 uses that one tempo with librosa's tightness of 100, so it cannot follow a tempo change.
note.rhythm.3: R3 uses 4.5 s Fourier tempogram windows, limited to ±18% of the local tempo track. Downbeats assume 4/4 and pick the bar phase with the most low-frequency onsets and chord changes.
note.rhythm.4: Sections use beat-length units when the pulse is clear, otherwise short blocks. Features are median-filtered over half the kernel, and the kernel spans 4 to 16 units each side.
note.rhythm.5: Neural beat trackers (madmom, Beat This!) are more accurate on real music but need trained models. They make a good offline reference rather than something to port to C#.
note.effects.title: Effects methods
note.effects.1: Spectral tools use a short-time Fourier transform with Hann windows at 75% overlap (1024 points for clips under 6 s, 2048 otherwise) and real per-bin gains, so phase is kept.
note.effects.2: De-harsh suppresses peaks more than 2 dB above a sixth-octave smoothed spectrum, weighted to 0.8–10 kHz, plus a top-end tilt when sharpness exceeds 1.75 acum. A gate driven by the harshness factor switches it on; release is 60 ms.
note.effects.3: Layer remix applies soft Wiener masks built from the NMF layers, interpolated from 40 mel bands to FFT bins. Attack and body uses median-filter separation (Fitzgerald 2010), 17 frames by 17 bins.
note.effects.4: Loudness matching uses ITU-R BS.1770 integrated loudness with its standard gates. Every output is lowered if it would clip.
note.sfx.title: Sound-effect methods
note.sfx.1: Events come from level re-attacks (8 dB within 15 ms) plus spectral onsets for new layers. Runs of three or more similar onsets closer than 0.4 s become one iterative event.
note.sfx.2: Tags follow Schaeffer's typology. N means more than half the loudness is pitched (YIN aperiodicity under 0.25, pitch above 60 Hz), Y means pitch or brightness glides, X means everything else. ′ marks events under 0.2 s and ″ marks grains or 8 to 40 Hz pulsing.
note.sfx.3: Attack, effective duration and temporal centre follow the Timbre Toolbox (simplified: 20% to 90% attack). Dynamic profiles follow Peeters and Deruty.
note.sfx.4: Thresholds were tuned on the built-in kit (24 of 25 tags) and then calibrated on real recordings with a held-out half; the kit score is optimistic.
guide.c1.name: C1 Loudness
guide.c1.reveal: Level weighted the way ears weight it, comparable across assets (BS.1770 K-weighting, −60 to 0 LUFS)
guide.c1.mislead: A sustained pad and a drum fill at the same loudness look identical
guide.c2.name: C2 Activity
guide.c2.reveal: Busyness at equal loudness: fills, grooves, bursts, a groove entering under an unchanged level
guide.c2.mislead: Dense rolls buried under a riser can read calm; tremolo and granular textures read busy
guide.c3.name: C3 Arousal
guide.c3.reveal: A single energy estimate: punchy, dynamic passages above compressed, static ones
guide.c3.mislead: Stays close to loudness; its noisiness term rewards hiss, wind and rain
guide.c4.name: C4 Harshness
guide.c4.reveal: Rough, sharp, alarm-like moments raised above smooth sounds of equal loudness
guide.c4.mislead: Bright masters are raised everywhere; hats and hiss add sharpness
guide.c5.name: C5 Tension
guide.c5.reveal: Build-ups, climaxes and releases, including tension rising on a loudness plateau
guide.c5.mislead: Short SFX and static loops give it nothing to integrate; abrupt entries count as builds
guide.c6.name: C6 Harmony
guide.c6.reveal: Clusters, suspensions, modulations and resolutions at constant dynamics
guide.c6.mislead: Meaningless on drums, noise and SFX (gated to zero); the least validated curve
guide.c7.name: C7 Novelty
guide.c7.reveal: Section changes, drops, new layers, a single event inside an ambience
guide.c7.mislead: Repetition reads calm after a few bars; spiky by nature
row.d3.auto: Picks height and colour by asset class.
row.c1.name: Loudness
row.c1.desc: K-weighted level in LUFS, absolute scale from −60 to 0.
row.c2.name: Activity
row.c2.desc: Spectral change where energy rises (positive spectral flux) plus onsets per second. Independent of level.
row.c3.name: Arousal
row.c4.name: Harshness-weighted loudness
row.c4.desc: Loudness raised by sharpness, roughness and fluctuation (Zwicker annoyance form).
row.c5.name: Tension
row.c5.desc: Integrated trends of loudness, sharpness, roughness and harmony (Farbood model).
row.c6.name: Harmonic tension
row.c6.desc: Chroma dissonance, distance from key and chord change (tonal interval vectors).
row.c7.name: Novelty
row.c7.desc: Spectral surprise beyond what loudness explains. Ticks mark the strongest new events.
row.r1.name: Events
row.r1.desc: Onsets, where the sound starts, and where it has fallen 30 dB below its peak. Works for any asset.
row.r2.name: Beat tracker
row.r2.desc: Dynamic programming over onsets at one global tempo (Ellis 2007). Thick lines are downbeats, assuming 4/4.
row.r3.name: Local pulse
row.r3.desc: Predominant local pulse (Grosche & Müller 2011). Follows tempo changes; peaks are beats, height scaled by clarity.
row.r4.name: Pulse clarity and tempo
row.r4.desc: Height: how regular the onsets are over 8 s. Colour: local tempo, grey where there is no clear pulse.
row.x1.name: Spectral silhouette
row.x1.desc: Height is loudness. Inside, colour shows where the energy sits: low frequencies at the centre, high at the edges.
row.x2.name: Layers
row.x2.desc: Up to three spectral components found by non-negative matrix factorisation, coloured by centre frequency. A sweep splits into consecutive layers.
row.x3.name: Pitch and brightness
row.x3.desc: Solid line: pitch where the sound is tonal. Dotted: spectral centroid. Log scale, 50 Hz at the bottom to 10 kHz at the top.
row.x4.name: Envelope
row.x4.desc: Loudness coloured by phase: attack, body within 12 dB of the peak, tail down to −45 dB. Tick: temporal centre.
row.x5.name: Sound objects
row.x5.desc: Events tagged with Schaeffer's typology: N tonal, X noisy, Y gliding; ′ impulse, ″ iterative.
row.x6.name: Space
row.x6.desc: Line: pan, left up and right down. Band: width, how different the two channels are.
row.x7.name: Asset checks
row.x7.desc: Clipping, DC offset, silence at either end, a non-zero first sample, a cut tail, loop seams.
row.s1.name: Structural novelty
row.s1.desc: How different the next few seconds are from the last few (Foote 2000, on timbre, chroma, level and activity). Lines are boundaries.
row.s2.name: Sections
row.s2.desc: Segments between boundaries, lettered by similarity. The same letter means returning material.
row.n1.name: Impulsiveness
row.n1.desc: Spectral kurtosis (machine diagnostics). Line at 0 is noise; down to −1 is a steady tone; up is clicks and crackle, coloured by the band that carries them. Dashed: the value that noise would give in this window.
row.n2.name: Repetition rate
row.n2.desc: Envelope spectrum per band (machine diagnostics): height is how clearly the level repeats, colour the rate from 0.5 Hz (dark) to 150 Hz (light). Firing rates, rattles, footsteps.
row.n3.name: Event statistics
row.n3.desc: STA/LTA trigger from seismology: each bar is an event from trigger to release, height its peak. Labels give rate, burstiness (−1 regular, 0 random, above 0 clustered) and the b-value (many small vs few big).
row.n4.name: Spectral motion
row.n4.desc: Optimal-transport velocity on a log-frequency axis: up is rising (risers, sweeps, Doppler), down falling, scale ±6 oct/s. Shaded: reshaping that is not a shift.
row.n5.name: Periodicity
row.n5.desc: Cepstral peak prominence (voice science): high for voiced, buzzing or pitched sound, without a pitch tracker. Line: phase coherence, 1 for stable partials, near 0 for noise and diffuse reverb.
row.n6.name: Arrow of time
row.n6.desc: Third-moment asymmetry of the log envelope: up for impacts and plucks (fast rise, slow fall), down for swells and reversed sounds, centre for anything that would sound the same backwards.
row.n7.name: Interest
row.n7.desc: Information dynamics (Abdallah & Plumbley) on timbre symbols: height is predictive information, high when what you hear changes what comes next. Line: learning, high when material is new, falling as it repeats.
row.n8.name: Recurrence
row.n8.desc: How often this moment's timbre and harmony recur elsewhere in the file. Line: laminarity, 1 while a state is held (drone, held chord, steady noise).
row.n9.name: Decay and material
row.n9.desc: Decay time (T60 from band decays, log scale 20 ms to 5 s) for each impact, coloured by Klatzky damping: blue damped (rubber, wood), green glass-like, orange metal-like, grey not modal. Reverb reads as metal.
row.d1.name: Energy
row.d2.name: Tension arc
row.d2.desc: Height tension (C5), colour harshness factor (C4), novelty ticks.
row.d3.name: Asset thumbnail
row.d5.name: SFX thumbnail
row.d5.desc: Spectral silhouette (X1) with event ticks (X5) and the pitch line where the sound is tonal (X3).
row.d4.name: Structure overlay
row.d4.desc: Height loudness (C1), colour activity (C2), line harmonic tension (C6), top band sections (S2), bar lines (R2), ticks novelty (C7).

lib.look.auto.name: Automatic
lib.look.auto.desc: Sound effects: harshness as colour, activity as the line, events. Music: activity as colour, tension as the line, sections, downbeats.
lib.look.plain.name: Waveform only
lib.look.plain.desc: The waveform without analysis, for comparison.
lib.look.spectrum.name: Spectrogram
lib.look.spectrum.desc: A standard spectrogram (mel scale, 40 Hz to 16 kHz), for comparison.
lib.look.structure.name: Structure
lib.look.structure.desc: Sections, structural change (up: entry, down: fall or break) and the local pulse under a plain waveform.
lib.look.rhythm.name: Rhythm
lib.look.rhythm.desc: Activity as colour, the local pulse, beats and downbeats.
lib.look.tension.name: Tension
lib.look.tension.desc: Harshness as colour, tension as the line, sections.
lib.look.events.name: Events
lib.look.events.desc: Harshness as colour, activity in a lane, events marked.
lib.look.lanes.name: Separate lanes
lib.look.lanes.desc: Plain waveform with loudness, activity and harshness each in its own lane (no colour mixing).
lib.look.shapes.name: Curves as waveforms
lib.look.shapes.desc: No waveform: loudness, activity and harshness each drawn like a waveform, mirrored around its middle.
lib.look.overlay.name: Curves over the waveform
lib.look.overlay.desc: Activity and harshness drawn like waveforms on top of the waveform itself, to compare their shapes directly.
lib.look.horizon.name: Horizon lanes
lib.look.horizon.desc: Loudness, activity and harshness as horizon charts: compact lanes that keep detail at small heights.
lib.look.specstructure.name: Spectrogram and structure
lib.look.specstructure.desc: The spectrogram with sections, structural change and downbeats.
lib.look.overview.name: Music overview
lib.look.overview.desc: Curves only, overlaid and mirrored like a waveform: local pulse, activity and recurrence, with sections, bar lines and novelty marks.
lib.look.character.name: Sound character
lib.look.character.desc: For sound effects. Curves only, overlaid and mirrored like a waveform: where the hits are (onset strength), harshness and impulsiveness (clicks, cracks, crackle), with onsets marked.
lib.look.surprise.name: Hits and surprise
lib.look.surprise.desc: For sound effects. As Sound character, with spectral surprise (where the sound turns into something new) in place of impulsiveness.
lib.look.hits.name: Hits and pulse
lib.look.hits.desc: The waveform with onset strength (where the hits are) and the local pulse as lanes, beats and bar lines.
lib.look.sculpted.name: Waveform as loud as it sounds
lib.look.sculpted.desc: The waveform's envelope follows perceived loudness (a dB-like scale) while its detail stays; colour shows harshness, with the ordinary peak outline for comparison.
lib.legend.heightNoWave: (shapes the waveform; add it to see)
lib.legend.signed: (up: entry, down: fall or break, centred: same level)
lib.tool.cleanup.name: Clean up for export
lib.tool.cleanup.desc: Fixes what the asset checks find: removes DC offset, rebuilds clipped peaks, trims silence, adds fades where the file clicks or the tail was cut, folds identical channels to mono, and normalises the peak.
lib.tool.deharsh.name: De-harsh
lib.tool.deharsh.desc: Suppresses narrow resonances between 0.8 and 10 kHz and tilts down the top end while the harshness model (sharpness, roughness and fluctuation in Zwicker's annoyance form) is high. "Harshest moments of this file" acts on the top of the file's own harshness range, so it works on mixes; "Only harsh sounds (absolute)" uses the absolute scale, where most music never qualifies; "Always" ignores the model. The detector can be switched to the level in the same frequency range, which makes it a conventional dynamic EQ, for comparison. The second result is what was removed, raised for listening.
lib.tool.layers.name: Layer remix
lib.tool.layers.desc: Rebalances the layers found by NMF (row X2) with soft Wiener masks: lift the casing ring, drop the sub, and so on.
lib.tool.hpss.name: Attack and body
lib.tool.hpss.desc: Splits each moment into percussive and sustained energy with median filtering (Fitzgerald 2010) and sets their levels separately: a transient shaper that follows content, not the envelope.
lib.tool.tension.name: Tension shaper
lib.tool.tension.desc: Turns the tension curve (C5) into gain and brightness automation. Positive contrast makes build-ups rise and releases fall further; negative contrast flattens them.
lib.tool.loop.name: Loop maker
lib.tool.loop.desc: Finds the start and end points whose surroundings match best (on downbeats when the beat is clear), moves them to zero crossings and renders an equal-power seam, so the result wraps without a click.
lib.tool.vars.name: Variations
lib.tool.vars.desc: Makes copies that differ the way repeated game sounds should: random layer balance, reordered grains inside iterative events, and a small pitch change.
lib.tool.tailverb.name: Reverb on the tails
lib.tool.tailverb.desc: Sends only the tails of the events into a reverb: each hit from its peak to the end of its decay, so the attack stays dry and punchy and the tail blooms. No EQ can do this, because the tool adds new energy after each sound and spreads it in time.
lib.tool.drive.name: Drive the hits
lib.tool.drive.desc: Saturates only the events (their attacks, their bodies, or all of them) and leaves the rest clean. The saturated part is held at the original level, so what changes is the harmonics, which no EQ can add, not the loudness.
lib.tool.ring.name: Ring time
lib.tool.ring.desc: Changes how long each event rings, relative to its own peak: longer for metal and glass, shorter for wood and cardboard. Higher partials can ring longer or shorter than lower ones, which moves the material read by the decay descriptor (N9). An EQ sets the same gain at every level; this sets it by how far each partial has decayed since its event's peak.
lib.tool.level.name: Level the events
lib.tool.level.desc: Evens out how loud the events are (footsteps, impacts, a burst of shots, debris) with one gain per event, changed only in the moment before each event starts. A compressor reaching the same evenness turns attacks down and makes the background pump; this leaves every event's attack and decay as it was.
lib.tool.mono.name: Fold to mono
lib.tool.mono.desc: Folds stereo to mono without the losses of a plain (L+R)/2: per frequency, the right channel is turned to the left channel's phase before summing, and the sum is brought back to the channels' energy. Each attack the analysis finds is folded in the time domain with its own delay and polarity between the channels, so there is no pre-echo. The report names the bands and events that cancel in a plain sum, which doubles as a mono-compatibility check. The second result is the plain sum, for comparison.
lib.tool.widen.name: Widen the tails
lib.tool.widen.desc: Makes stereo from mono (or widens stereo) by adding a decorrelated copy of the sound (a velvet-noise decorrelator) to the side, only after the attacks the analysis finds: attacks stay centred and punchy, tails and background open up, and the lows stay centred. Only the side changes, so (L+R)/2 gives back the original exactly: the result is fully mono-compatible.
